newsitem.title: CUBA: Vatican envoy meets Cuban Communist Party official.
newsitem.headline: Vatican envoy meets Cuban Communist Party official.

text.p: Cuba's ruling Communist Party told visiting Vatican Foreign Minister Jean Louis Tauran on Monday that there was a mutual will to resolve problems in relations between Havana and the Roman Catholic Church.
Tauran, who arrived on Friday for a five-day visit, met Caridad Diego, head of the party's religious affairs department, for talks on Monday at the party central committee headquarters in Havana.
In brief welcoming comments, Diego told Tauran "we will be able to deal with some concrete problems in the relationship between the Catholic church in Cuba and our state."

"I'm sure we will find formulas (to deal with these problems) because there is a mutual willingness," Diego said. "I think this a good moment, there is a favourable climate in the normalisation of relations," she added.
The rest of their talks were closed to reporters.

The papal envoy, who is an archbishop, is the first Vatican foreign minister to be invited to Cuba by the government. His visit comes at a time of clearly improved relations between authorities and the church.

Tauran, who pleased his hosts on Saturday by condemning the longstanding U.S. embargo against Cuba, said at a mass on Sunday the Vatican would still like to see the church enjoying a wider public space on the island.
He gave as examples issues such as delays granting visas for foreign priests and nuns and also what he saw as the need for a wider area of work for the church charity, Caritas.
However Tauran has, at least in public, confined his remarks to the work of the church in Cuba and has made no comments on the island's political system.

His visit comes amid speculation Cuban President Fidel Castro may meet the pontiff if he travels to Rome for a summit on food being organised by the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation from Nov. 13 to 17. Diplomatic sources in Rome have said if Castro does meet the pope he will probably invite him to Cuba next year.

Tauran, who was due to depart on Tuesday, was likely to meet Castro during his stay, but a meeting has not been officially announced. So far Tauran has held talks with Foreign Minister Roberto Robaina and parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon, as well as local church leaders.
Speaking at the mass on Sunday, Tauran said he was hopeful the pope would visit the island to help "set the seal on a climate of religious freedom and confidence (in Cuba)".

Cuban authorities have moved in recent years to improve relations with Christian churches, strained since Castro's 1959 revolution. But tensions with the Catholic Church persisted, mainly over periodic calls by the bishops for political change.
But there has been a clear improvement in recent months. Cuba's Cardinal Jaime Ortega said in September that comments on religion in a recent Communist Party document were encouraging.
